article.title: FCC Adds Foreign-Made Humanoid and Quadruped Robots to Its Covered List, Citing National Security Risks From China
article.summary: The FCC blocked new imports of foreign-made humanoid and quadruped robots and power inverters, a move aimed at China, which ships more than 85% of the world's humanoid robots.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

The Federal Communications Commission on July 28 added foreign-produced humanoid and quadruped robots, along with foreign-produced connected power inverters, to its Covered List, blocking new models from receiving the equipment authorization required to enter the U.S. market, according to the [FCC's own fact sheet](https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DOC-423682A1.txt). The agency defines the newly covered category of "advanced robotic devices" as ["mobile robots, such as humanoids and quadrupeds,"](https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DOC-423682A1.txt) and the action is widely seen as targeting China, which dominates global humanoid robot production, according to [Fortune](https://fortune.com/2026/07/29/chinas-robot-makers-shipped-25x-more-units-than-u-s-rivals-in-2025-so-america-banned-them/).

## What We Know

- The FCC's fact sheet states the reasoning for robots directly: ["The networked capabilities of advanced robotic systems create extensive vulnerabilities and vectors for attacks that can manipulate the data and physical operation of the advanced robotic system,"](https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DOC-423682A1.txt) and separately warns that a lack of a secure domestic supply chain for power inverters poses risks to "U.S. economic and national security."
- According to [CBS News](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/humanoid-robots-imports-us-ban-china-national-security-concerns/), a White House task force concluded that foreign-built robots pose "a cybersecurity risk that threatens the security of critical infrastructure" and "the safety and security" of U.S. residents.
- FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said the action was designed to ["secure America's critical supply chains,"](https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DOC-423682A1.txt) with [Robotics and Automation News](https://roboticsandautomationnews.com/2026/07/29/fcc-updates-covered-list-to-include-foreign-produced-advanced-robotic-devices-and-power-inverters/103658/) reporting his full statement: "Following President Trump's leadership, the FCC will continue to do our part to secure America's critical supply chains and, with today's action, the FCC is acting in lock step with our national security agencies to do just that."
- The measure is forward-looking only. According to [Forbes](https://www.forbes.com/sites/johnkoetsier/2026/07/28/united-states-bans-chinese-humanoid--quadruped-robots-citing-national-security/), products already authorized before the order remain available for sale, retailers may continue distributing previously cleared models, and the order does not recall existing consumer devices.
- Manufacturers can still seek a "Conditional Approval" exemption, according to the FCC and [Robotics and Automation News](https://roboticsandautomationnews.com/2026/07/29/fcc-updates-covered-list-to-include-foreign-produced-advanced-robotic-devices-and-power-inverters/103658/): through the Department of War for robots, or the Department of Homeland Security for power inverters, with applications submitted to conditional-approvals@fcc.gov.
- China dominates the market the rule targets. Both [CBS News](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/humanoid-robots-imports-us-ban-china-national-security-concerns/) and [Fortune](https://fortune.com/2026/07/29/chinas-robot-makers-shipped-25x-more-units-than-u-s-rivals-in-2025-so-america-banned-them/) put China's share of the global humanoid robot market at roughly 85%. Fortune reports that of the around 15,000 humanoid robots shipped globally in 2025, Chinese manufacturers Unitree and AGIBOT each shipped more than 5,000, while U.S. counterparts like Tesla and Figure AI each shipped only a few hundred or less.
- China's government has pushed back. According to [CBS News](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/humanoid-robots-imports-us-ban-china-national-security-concerns/), China's Foreign Ministry accused Washington of "overstretching the concept of national security to suppress Chinese companies" and said China would take "all measures necessary" to defend the interests of Chinese businesses. Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters at a regular press conference in Beijing on Wednesday: "Protectionism does not make the U.S. more competitive, and it will only hurt the interests of U.S. companies and consumers."
- The order lands just weeks before a planned meeting between President Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping. [Fortune](https://fortune.com/2026/07/29/chinas-robot-makers-shipped-25x-more-units-than-u-s-rivals-in-2025-so-america-banned-them/) reports the measures "are likely to test relations with Beijing ahead of a planned U.S. visit by Chinese leader Xi Jinping to meet with U.S. President Donald Trump in September."

## What We Don't Know

- The FCC's own materials do not name China explicitly in the Covered List determination; the practical impact on Chinese manufacturers stems from their dominant share of the humanoid and quadruped robot market rather than an explicit country designation in the order's text.
- It is not yet clear how many Conditional Approval applications, if any, have been filed with the Department of War or Department of Homeland Security, or how quickly such exemptions might be processed.
- The precise commercial impact on U.S. companies that currently resell or integrate foreign-made robots — beyond the stated exemption for already-authorized models — has not been detailed in available reporting.

## Analysis

The rule adds humanoid and quadruped robots to a Covered List mechanism the FCC has previously used against foreign telecommunications equipment, extending a trade-and-security framework built for network hardware to a physical robotics market where, per Fortune's shipment figures, Chinese firms are shipping several times more units than their American counterparts. Because the order is forward-looking and existing devices are unaffected, its near-term effect is less about pulling robots off U.S. shop floors than about foreclosing them from future decisions — reviews such as this one determining which vendors are eligible when American businesses next purchase warehouse, security, or industrial robots at scale.
